titulo: The bill comes due: Europe's public debt after the pandemic and the energy crisis

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: Governments across the continent borrowed on an unprecedented scale to shield households and firms from two successive shocks. Now, with interest rates far higher than they were a few years ago and a revamped set of fiscal rules finally in force, the bill is coming due. The question is no longer whether Europe must put its public finances in order, but how quickly, by what means and at whose expense.

When the pandemic struck in early 2020, European finance ministers did something that would have been unthinkable a decade earlier: they suspended the fiscal rules altogether. The so-called general escape clause of the Stability and Growth Pact allowed capitals to spend whatever it took to keep their economies on life support. Furlough schemes paid the wages of millions of workers, state-backed loans kept otherwise viable companies afloat and health systems received emergency funding. The result was a jump in public debt of a size rarely seen in peacetime. Across the euro area, the debt-to-GDP ratio climbed by more than ten percentage points in a single year, to close to 100% of output.

Just as the recovery was gathering pace, a second blow arrived. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sent gas and electricity prices soaring, and governments once again reached for their chequebooks. This time the support was less carefully designed. Rather than targeting the most vulnerable, many countries opted for blanket measures such as caps on retail energy prices, cuts in fuel duties and subsidies that benefited wealthy and poor households alike. Economists broadly agree that such untargeted aid was expensive, blunted the price signal needed to encourage energy saving and, in some cases, proved surprisingly difficult to withdraw once wholesale prices had fallen back.

Paradoxically, the debt ratios of many countries actually improved in 2022 and 2023. The explanation lies in the arithmetic of inflation. Because debt is measured against nominal GDP, a burst of rising prices inflates the denominator while leaving the stock of existing bonds, issued at fixed and often very low rates, largely untouched. Inflation, in other words, quietly eroded part of the real value of what governments owed. Yet this was a one-off windfall rather than a lasting solution. Bondholders, and the central bank that had to fight that inflation, were never going to allow the trick to be repeated indefinitely.

That fight has changed the landscape. Between mid-2022 and late 2023 the European Central Bank raised its key rates at the fastest pace in its history, bringing to an end an era in which some governments could borrow for ten years at negative yields. Although the ECB has since begun to ease, nobody expects a return to the ultra-low rates of the previous decade. As old bonds mature and are refinanced at higher coupons, the average cost of servicing public debt is rising slowly but relentlessly. For heavily indebted states, interest payments are already crowding out spending on education, infrastructure and defence.

The picture, however, is far from uniform. On one side stand countries such as Italy and Greece, whose debt still exceeds 130% of GDP, alongside France and Belgium, where it hovers above 100% and deficits remain stubbornly wide. On the other sit several northern and central European economies, including the Netherlands and some of the Nordic states, with ratios comfortably below the 60% reference value. Spain and Portugal occupy an intermediate position: both have reduced their ratios markedly since the peak of the pandemic, helped by robust growth and buoyant tax revenues, with Portugal making particularly rapid progress. This divergence matters, because a single monetary policy must serve members with very different fiscal vulnerabilities.

It is against this backdrop that the European Union rewrote its fiscal rulebook. The reformed framework, which entered into force in 2024, keeps the familiar headline thresholds of a 3% deficit and a debt ratio of 60%, but changes almost everything else. Instead of uniform annual targets, each government now agrees a medium-term plan, typically covering four years, built around a single operational indicator: the growth of net primary expenditure. Countries that commit to reforms and investment can obtain a longer adjustment path of up to seven years. The aim is to make the rules more realistic, more tailored to national circumstances and, crucially, more likely to be respected.

Critics are not convinced. Some fiscal hawks argue that the new system grants too much discretion to the European Commission and leaves room for political bargaining, the very weakness that undermined the old pact. From the opposite camp, many economists warn that the safeguards added at the insistence of more frugal member states, including minimum annual reductions in debt and deficits, will force premature austerity on countries that can least afford it. Others point out that the debt sustainability analysis at the heart of the framework relies on projections of growth and interest rates that are, by their nature, highly uncertain.

Meanwhile, the list of spending demands keeps growing. The green transition requires vast public and private investment in grids, renewable energy and building renovation. Russia's war has convinced governments that they must spend far more on defence, and EU leaders have agreed to give military outlays additional flexibility under the rules. Ageing populations will push up pension and healthcare costs over the coming decades. And the joint borrowing undertaken for the NextGenerationEU recovery fund will have to be repaid from the late 2020s onwards, raising the awkward question of whether the Union should create genuine new resources of its own.

Can these competing pressures be reconciled? Optimists stress that the most painless way to stabilise debt is to grow out of it. As long as the economy expands faster than the interest rate paid on the debt, a government can see its ratio fall even while running a modest primary deficit. The real difficulty is that Europe's trend growth is weak, held back by sluggish productivity and shrinking workforces. Structural reforms, a deeper single market and a genuine capital markets union could lift that growth rate, but their benefits take years to materialise, while bond markets can lose patience in a matter of days, as the United Kingdom discovered in the autumn of 2022.

Pessimists, by contrast, fear a slow-motion squeeze. If governments postpone adjustment until markets force their hand, the eventual consolidation could be abrupt and politically explosive, feeding the populist movements that have already gained ground in several capitals. The memory of the euro-area debt crisis of the early 2010s, when spreads on southern bonds widened dramatically and austerity deepened recessions, still shapes the debate. The ECB now has a dedicated instrument to counter disorderly market movements, but it comes with strict conditions and has never been tested in a real emergency.

Perhaps the most sensible path lies between these extremes: a gradual, credible adjustment that protects productive investment, relies more on the quality of spending than on blunt cuts, and broadens tax bases rather than simply raising rates. The pandemic and the energy crisis showed that fiscal firepower is invaluable when disaster strikes. The lesson of the coming decade may be that such firepower has to be rebuilt in calmer times. A government that enters the next crisis with lower debt will, quite simply, have more room to protect its citizens.
titulo_es: Llega la factura: la deuda pública europea tras la pandemia y la crisis energética
resumen_es: Análisis de cómo la pandemia y la crisis energética dispararon la deuda pública en Europa y de los dilemas que plantean ahora los tipos de interés más altos, las nuevas reglas fiscales de la UE y las crecientes necesidades de gasto.

ideas_clave.idea: After two crises financed with massive borrowing, Europe now has to decide the pace, instruments and distribution of fiscal adjustment.
The pandemic led to the suspension of EU fiscal rules and a sharp rise in debt, and the energy shock of 2022 brought further, often poorly targeted, support measures.
Inflation temporarily lowered debt ratios, but the ECB's rapid tightening has ended the era of cheap money and interest costs are gradually squeezing other spending.
Debt levels differ widely between member states, which complicates a single monetary policy.
The reformed EU framework of 2024 keeps the 3% and 60% thresholds but relies on national medium-term plans based on net primary expenditure, with longer paths for reforming countries.
The reform is criticised both for being too lax and discretionary and for imposing excessive austerity through its safeguards and uncertain projections.
New spending needs, such as the green transition, defence, ageing and the repayment of joint EU debt, add to the pressure.
Optimists rely on growth outpacing interest rates, whereas pessimists fear delayed and abrupt adjustment with political costs, recalling the crisis of the 2010s.
The author favours a gradual and credible consolidation focused on spending quality and broader tax bases, so as to rebuild fiscal room for future crises.

resumen_modelo: The article examines the state of Europe's public finances after two consecutive shocks. To cushion the impact of the pandemic, the EU suspended its fiscal rules in 2020, allowing governments to finance job-retention schemes, guaranteed loans and health spending; as a consequence, euro-area debt rose to roughly the size of annual output. The energy crisis triggered by the war in Ukraine then prompted another wave of support which, being largely untargeted, proved costly and hard to reverse. Although inflation briefly reduced debt ratios by boosting nominal GDP, this relief was temporary. Moreover, the sharpest monetary tightening in the ECB's history has put an end to near-zero borrowing costs, so that interest payments are progressively displacing productive spending, particularly in highly indebted countries such as Italy, Greece, France or Belgium, while others remain well below the 60% benchmark. In response, the EU adopted new fiscal rules in 2024. While maintaining the traditional reference values, the framework is based on country-specific medium-term plans that cap the growth of net primary spending and allow longer adjustment periods in exchange for reforms. Nevertheless, it is criticised from both sides: some consider it too discretionary, others fear that its safeguards will impose premature austerity. At the same time, spending pressures linked to climate, defence, ageing and the repayment of joint EU borrowing keep mounting. Whereas optimists hope that growth will outpace interest rates, pessimists warn of an abrupt and politically dangerous adjustment. The author concludes that a gradual, credible consolidation that preserves investment is the wisest option, as it would restore room for manoeuvre before the next crisis.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: During the pandemic, the EU fiscal rules were relaxed only for the countries hardest hit by the virus.
preguntas.cita: they suspended the fiscal rules altogether
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que las reglas se suspendieron por completo («altogether») mediante la cláusula general de escape, no solo para algunos países. El detalle cambiado es el alcance de la suspensión.

preguntas.enunciado: Elige la opción correcta según el texto.
preguntas.pregunta: What is the main criticism the article makes of the energy support measures adopted in 2022?
opciones: They arrived too late to help households
They were not targeted at those most in need
They were financed exclusively by the EU budget
They focused only on industrial users
respuestas: They were not targeted at those most in need
preguntas.cita: Rather than targeting the most vulnerable, many countries opted for blanket measures
preguntas.explicacion: La crítica central es que las ayudas fueron generales («blanket») y beneficiaron a ricos y pobres por igual. El texto no habla de retraso, de financiación europea ni de que se limitaran a la industria.

preguntas.enunciado: Elige la opción correcta según el texto.
preguntas.pregunta: Why did debt ratios improve in many countries in 2022 and 2023?
opciones: Because inflation raised nominal GDP while existing debt stayed largely unchanged
Because the ECB bought most of the outstanding debt
Because tax rates were raised across Europe
respuestas: Because inflation raised nominal GDP while existing debt stayed largely unchanged
preguntas.cita: a burst of rising prices inflates the denominator while leaving the stock of existing bonds, issued at fixed and often very low rates, largely untouched
preguntas.explicacion: El efecto se explica por la aritmética de la inflación: sube el PIB nominal (denominador) y la deuda emitida a tipo fijo no cambia. El texto no atribuye la mejora a recortes, compras del BCE ni subidas de impuestos.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 4 una palabra o expresión que signifique «ganancia inesperada, beneficio caído del cielo».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “an unexpected gain”.
preguntas.cita: this was a one-off windfall rather than a lasting solution
preguntas.explicacion: «Windfall» designa un beneficio inesperado; aquí, la reducción de la ratio de deuda que trajo la inflación sin que los gobiernos hicieran nada.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The ECB's rate increases between 2022 and 2023 were the fastest in its history.
preguntas.cita: raised its key rates at the fastest pace in its history
preguntas.explicacion: El texto lo afirma expresamente: el BCE subió los tipos al ritmo más rápido de su historia entre mediados de 2022 y finales de 2023.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 5 una expresión que signifique «desplazar, restar espacio a» (otro gasto).
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning “taking resources away from”.
preguntas.cita: interest payments are already crowding out spending on education, infrastructure and defence
preguntas.explicacion: «To crowd out» es el término económico para el efecto expulsión o desplazamiento: el pago de intereses deja menos margen para otras partidas.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Spain's debt ratio has fallen faster than Portugal's since the pandemic.
preguntas.cita: with Portugal making particularly rapid progress
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice lo contrario: ambos países han reducido su ratio, pero es Portugal el que ha avanzado con especial rapidez.

preguntas.enunciado: Elige la opción correcta según el texto.
preguntas.pregunta: Under the reformed EU fiscal framework, what is the single operational indicator?
opciones: The growth of net primary expenditure
The annual reduction of the debt ratio by one twentieth
The interest burden as a share of GDP
respuestas: The growth of net primary expenditure
preguntas.cita: built around a single operational indicator: the growth of net primary expenditure
preguntas.explicacion: El nuevo marco gira en torno al crecimiento del gasto primario neto. El saldo estructural y la regla de una veinteava parte pertenecían al marco anterior, y la carga de intereses no se menciona como indicador.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Spain has already obtained a seven-year adjustment path under the new rules.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto explica que los países que se comprometen a reformas e inversiones pueden obtener una senda de hasta siete años, pero no dice qué países la han conseguido ni menciona a España en ese contexto.

preguntas.enunciado: Elige la opción correcta según el texto.
preguntas.pregunta: What do some economists fear about the safeguards included in the new rules?
opciones: That they will be ignored by the Commission
That they will impose austerity too early on vulnerable countries
That they will encourage excessive public investment
That they will make the ECB less independent
respuestas: That they will impose austerity too early on vulnerable countries
preguntas.cita: will force premature austerity on countries that can least afford it
preguntas.explicacion: Los economistas citados temen una austeridad prematura en los países más frágiles. La discrecionalidad de la Comisión es la crítica del otro bando, y no se habla de exceso de inversión ni de la independencia del BCE.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 9 una palabra que signifique «gastos» (sinónimo de «expenditure»).
preguntas.cita: EU leaders have agreed to give military outlays additional flexibility under the rules
preguntas.explicacion: «Outlays» es un sinónimo formal de gasto o desembolso, muy frecuente en prensa económica.

preguntas.pregunta: According to the optimists, under what condition can a country reduce its debt ratio without running a primary surplus, and why is this difficult for Europe?
respuestas: If the economy grows faster than the interest rate paid on its debt, the ratio can fall even with a small primary deficit. This is hard for Europe because its trend growth is weak due to low productivity and shrinking workforces.
preguntas.cita: As long as the economy expands faster than the interest rate paid on the debt, a government can see its ratio fall
preguntas.explicacion: Se pide la condición r < g y la razón del escepticismo: el escaso crecimiento potencial europeo. Una buena respuesta menciona ambas partes.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the author's own position, and what lesson does he or she draw from the recent crises?
respuestas: The author supports a gradual but credible adjustment that protects investment, improves the quality of spending and broadens tax bases. The lesson is that governments need to rebuild fiscal space in good times so they can respond forcefully to the next crisis.
preguntas.cita: Perhaps the most sensible path lies between these extremes: a gradual, credible adjustment that protects productive investment
preguntas.explicacion: La postura del autor aparece en el último párrafo: una vía intermedia. La lección es recuperar margen fiscal en tiempos tranquilos para poder actuar en la próxima crisis.

tribunal.pregunta: Could you summarise the two shocks that, according to the article, pushed up public debt in Europe?
tribunal.pista_es: Comprensión: identificar la pandemia y la crisis energética y el tipo de medidas de cada una.
ideas: Pandemic: suspension of the fiscal rules, furlough schemes, guaranteed loans
Energy crisis after the invasion of Ukraine: price caps, tax cuts, subsidies
Second wave of support was less targeted

tribunal.pregunta: Why does the article describe the effect of inflation on debt as a one-off windfall?
tribunal.pista_es: Explicar el mecanismo del denominador y por qué no puede repetirse.
ideas: Higher nominal GDP lowers the ratio
Fixed-rate bonds are not affected immediately
Central banks react by raising rates, so the effect cannot last

tribunal.pregunta: What are the main changes introduced by the reform of the EU fiscal framework?
tribunal.pista_es: Describir el nuevo marco: planes nacionales a medio plazo, indicador de gasto, sendas más largas.
ideas: Same 3% and 60% reference values
National medium-term fiscal-structural plans
Net primary expenditure as the operational indicator
Extension to seven years in exchange for reforms and investment

tribunal.pregunta: Do you think the new rules strike the right balance between flexibility and credibility?
tribunal.pista_es: Opinión argumentada recogiendo las críticas de ambos lados.
ideas: Ownership and realism versus discretion and bargaining
Safeguards may cause procyclical austerity
Credibility depends on enforcement by the Commission and the Council

tribunal.pregunta: How does Spain's fiscal position compare with that of other euro-area countries, and what challenges does it face?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar el texto con España: situación intermedia, crecimiento, gasto en pensiones e intereses.
ideas: Debt reduced since the pandemic thanks to growth and tax revenues
Still well above the 60% benchmark
Pressure from pensions and rising interest costs
Medium-term plan agreed with the Commission
